America needs new power lines far faster than it can build them.

Department of Energy studies imply the U.S. needs about 5,000 miles of new high-capacity transmission a year. The country built fewer than 900 miles in 2024. Most new data centers need a connection to that grid, so the pace of grid construction will set the pace of AI this decade.

Money alone cannot close that gap. Record utility spending has not shortened the 5 to 15 years it takes to permit and build a high-voltage line. A journeyman lineworker still takes about four years to train however much the job pays.

Existing lines can carry much more in the meantime. Restringing old towers with advanced wire can raise a line’s capacity by half or more within a few years. A Duke University study found today’s grid could absorb 76 GW of new load if data centers cut back just 0.25% of the time.

Until new lines catch up, the fastest gains will come from getting more out of the grid that already exists.

Following the Lumentum / Marvell deal: 

My opinion is that independent Western laser players, like $AAOI, $COHR, and $SIVE became a lot more strategically valuable. 

$MTSI and $SMTC should get some attention too as emerging laser players in 2027. 

If I had to guess: 

1. Companies competing against Marvell, or not in the $NVDA ecosystem bandwagon, such as $AMD, are likely going to rethink their relationship with $LITE.

If getting bottlenecked by Nvidia capacity agreements wasn't enough... Incentives around qualifying + bringing up other laser players, seems very necessary now. 

Since you generally don't want competitors like Marvell to have influence or visibility over your roadmaps, IP, capacity, pricing, etc. even if there is a "firewall".  

2. $MRVL acquiring Lumentum opened pandoras box in a way of acquiring a critical chokepoint all your competitors + buyers use. 

$LITE was used by your major hyperscalers and across AI supply chains. 

Now, your leaders might wonder if weaponizing capacity agreements might not be as effective.... If someone else can just buy the entire company. 

There's only a few major public merchant Western players out there, and I'm also sure many others will want to follow the Marvell / Broadcom route via vertical integration, given I think $MRVL saves around $1B+ in costs/year. 

So M&A premiums likely went up. 

$SMTC was actively looking to buy laser capacity via M&A so I'm sure they're looking at $SIVE given their 100M CW DFB laser expansion + tiny MC. 

$JBL also probably wants to vertically integrate down the road too so $SIVE is also an acquisition target for their 1.6T program. 

$AMD was looking for ELSFP + CW capacity given Nvidia bottlenecks, so I'm sure they've looked at $AAOI. 

can go on and on about other ASIC players (like in Taiwan) that likely are looking at vertical integration too.

Since multiple players use a small subset of laser suppliers, if competitors just go ahead and buys them... 

There's a lot pressure to M&A for their own supply chain defensibility. 

TLDR: Independent laser suppliers should capture a material strategic revaluation since $MRVL + $LITE, sets a new precedent + implications. 

We'll see what happens.

There's this saying back when I was doing Private Equity that

"Investment is like marriage"

That was certainly true in PE where an investment could last years and as an investor you're essentially required to support your portcos as much as you can

What's interesting is that crypto is starting to feel like marriage

Crypto used to feel like one night stand - a one and done kinda experience where you get in fast, get out fast, and then rotate onto the next trade

Now it's the other way around, "onchain businesses" are treating token holders like equity holders. And because of that, the onchain businesses are starting to be treated, valued, and priced like actual businesses. Onchain exchanges, inference platforms, yield venues, lending marketplaces 

While valuation multiples remain compressed, it's starting to make sense to value these "companies" based on their growth trajectory, based on their growth as a business and not on how hyped they can make it to be.

It feels like the bride and the groom are aligned and on the same page instead of one wanting to extract from the other as fast as possible

Pretty bullish
